items.abstract: <jats:p>Specializations of blood vasculature in the central nervous system (CNS), including the blood–brain barrier (BBB), neurovascular coupling, and perivascular spaces, maintain CNS homeostasis and become dysfunctional in disease and aging. Protein turnover, the process by which proteins are continually degraded and replaced, profoundly influences cell and tissue function and is dysregulated in aging and disease. Understanding the turnover of neurovascular proteins could provide insight into how the vasculature achieves both long-term structural stability and dynamic regulation. Vascular proteins, however, are underrepresented in previous studies of in vivo brain protein turnover. In this work, we used stable isotope labeling, nonenzymatic blood vessel enrichment, and high-resolution mass spectrometry-based proteomics to quantify the half-lives of brain vascular proteins in young adult and aged mice. We report half-life estimates for 1,358 proteins, including components of endothelial junctions, BBB transporters, astrocyte endfoot proteins, and vascular basement membrane proteins. We found that certain classes of proteins with related functions had similar half-lives, including BBB junctional proteins (~3 d), BBB transporters (~2 to 6 d), and most basement membrane components (>30 d). We also identified peptide motifs enriched in proteins with short and long half-lives and found differences in half-life distributions for cell type–specific proteomes. Finally, although we did not observe a global age-related shift in vascular protein turnover, we did identify specific proteins with increased or decreased half-lives in aging. This work establishes a high-quality database of neurovascular protein half-lives and provides a foundation for understanding how protein turnover contributes to neurovascular function and age-associated dysfunction.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Taphonomy, the study of environmental effects on decomposition and skeletonisation across different environments, requires an in-depth understanding of contextual variation. This study aimed to test the suitability of porcine taphonomic scoring criteria when applied to the human skeletal remains of individuals from the historic Koffiefontein and Witwatersrand Deep mines and to assess the effects of different burial environments on bone. The sample comprised 60 individuals and was divided into six skeletal regions and scored on six alterations: bone weathering, adipocere formation, acidic soil corrosion, depositional soil staining, plant activity and animal activity. Soil staining showed the most variation between the Koffiefontein and porcine groups, with Koffiefontein exhibiting unique artefact staining. Significant differences were found between the Koffiefontein and porcine groups for all alterations (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.026), except animal activity. Following these results, amendments were made to the scoring criteria to better fit patterns observed in human bone taphonomy, and taphonomic comparisons were then conducted between the two human groups to assess the effects of differential burial environments. Bone weathering and corrosion showed the most prominent differences between the human groups. Significant differences were found between the human groups in all dry bone alterations (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.035), except for soil staining. Variation in climatic conditions and burial microenvironments appears to underlie these taphonomic differences. Taken together, the findings indicate that the porcine scoring system is inadequate for characterising taphonomy in human remains, underscoring the need to account for the specific burial environment when interpreting taphonomic evidence.
                  </jats:p>
